newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe business, unions meet over strikes wave.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe business, unions meet over strikes wave.

text.p: Zimbabwe trade unions met private business leaders on Monday to try to end a wave of wildcat pay strikes.

Top officials from the two sides agreed at the start of the one-day conference that the strikes were undermining productivity and clouding the national investment climate, and highlighted shortcomings in the current process of labour disputes resolution.

Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU) Secretary-General Morgan Tsvangirai called on both industry and union leaders to negotiate a future that offered higher productivity, fair pay and working conditions, job security and sustainable economic growth.

He said the rise in industrial disputes was a sign that many workers sincerely believed that they were getting a raw deal from their employers and managers, while corporate leaders reaped the fruits of restructuring and down-sizing.

Tsvangirai added that there was a need to expand business and worker cooperation beyond the current preoccupation with wages and working conditions, to joint-union management, with a greater focus on higher economic growth.

Zimbabwe's agriculture-based economy has grown at an average 1.8 percent annually since 1990, against a population growth rate of about three percent, and Tsvangirai said the whole country had a responsibility for better and sustainable growth.

"What we are proposing is joint action in the expansion of the economic pie and resort to adversarial relations when it comes to dividing it," he told 200 delegates at the conference, jointly organised by the ZCTU and the Employers' Confederation of Zimbabwe (EMCOZ).

Zimbabwe has been rocked by a series of short wildcat strikes -- which have become an annual ritual -- from workers seeking to strengthen their negotiating positions for higher wage rises for the financial year starting in July.
Industries hit by the strikes include banking, textile and clothing, transport, and hotels and restaurants, where workers have been demanding annual pay increases of between 25 and 60 percent.

EMCOZ Executive Director Peter Kunjeku said the wage negotiations had been complicated by the fact that national unions -- authorised by law -- were negotiating for specific industries at one level, while workers' committees were demanding talks at enterprise level.
Many unions have demanded wage rises of between 24 and 30 percent, but workers' committees at enterprise level have asked for up 60 percent.

George Makings, a leading Zimbabwean labour consultant, also called for a clear allocation of responsibility, and for more labour disputes to be handled by arbitration instead of a labour tribunal which is currently battling with a three-year backlog of cases.
"As things stand now, we are all losers and we must look for a winning formula," he said.
